title: The Divided Kingdom
lead: After Solomon's death (about 931 BC) the ten northern tribes broke away from David's house and formed the kingdom of Israel, while Judah, with Benjamin, kept Jerusalem and David's line. The two kingdoms lived side by side, often at war, until Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BC. The prophets hoped for a reunion under one shepherd.

sections.b:
The split came at Shechem, when Rehoboam refused to lighten the yoke of forced labor and the northern tribes made Jeroboam king (1 Kings 12). Kings tells the two histories side by side, moving between them by synchronized dates (1 Kings 15–2 Kings 17). Israel had nine dynasties in about two hundred years, most ended by assassination; Judah kept David's line until the Babylonian exile. Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17); Judah fell to Babylon in 586 BC (2 Kings 25).

The prophets spoke to both. Amos and Hosea preached in the north; Isaiah and Micah in the south. Hosea and Ezekiel foresaw reunion: "one king will be king over them all, and they will no longer be two nations" (Ezekiel 37:22, fresh rendering; Hosea 1:11). Later, the Samaritans traced their descent to the northern tribes, and the New Testament tells of Jesus speaking to a Samaritan woman about worship that is neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem (John 4:20–24).
